item.text: I’ve confirmed the splitter respects quoted text and both `--` and `/* */` comments. I’m checking boundary cases now, because Python’s list formatting and `sqlparse.split` semantics will matter more than the nominal SQL examples.

The executable also treats backticks, bracketed identifiers, and doubled single quotes as semicolon-safe. I’m probing dollar-quoted blocks and escape formatting next, since those are the likeliest hidden regressions in a SQL splitter.

item.text: I found one non-trivial behavior: semicolons inside `BEGIN ... END;` blocks are not always statement boundaries. That means a naive quote/comment-aware splitter is still wrong for some procedural SQL, so I’m mapping the block rules before writing code.

item.text: I’m pinning down Python’s exact string representation now. `console.log` won’t match it: Python flips between single and double quotes to minimize escaping, so the Node side needs a real Python-style repr formatter instead of relying on JS defaults.

I found another `sqlparse` detail that affects splitting: a line comment after a terminating semicolon stays attached to the previous statement, but a block comment after that semicolon starts the next statement. I’m testing the exact boundary rules before I code them.
